articles.title: 'We're inundated' - Glasgow's struggle to house the homeless
articles.summary: Scott Crean has been homeless for the last year - and since Christmas has been staying in a hotel room in Glasgow.
articles.body:
Scott Crean is living out of a suitcase.

He's been homeless for the last year - and since Christmas has been staying in a hotel room in Glasgow.

In September 2025, the 37-year-old was among a record number people who were stuck in temporary accommodation in Glasgow and across Scotland.

Now the latest figures are set to be released amid fears that the problem is continuing to get worse.

Scott says he has been "in limbo" after being made redundant from his job at a charity shop and then made homeless after a family breakdown – all within the space of a few weeks last year.

"It's as if I'm stuck in a time I can't get out of... It's the waiting game that I can't stand," he said.

Scott showed us around his hotel room near the city's Trongate. It's a basic room with a queen-sized bed, sink and small shower room.

His clothes and personal effects are dotted round the cramped space, which is paid straight from his Universal Credit.

"Granted, it's nice... but I want my own home. The idea of living in a hotel doesn't live up to the hype," he said.

"At the end of the day, it's not somewhere I can decorate or call my own. It's living out of a suitcase. I don't feel comfortable here.

"Even through I've got a roof over my head, I want to be in my own home, paying my own rent, paying my electricity, paying my way."

Scott said he accepted an offer of a home in the Sandyhills area two weeks ago, but had not yet been told when he could view the property.

"It's frustrating, needing an answer and not getting it. Doesn't matter how many times you email or call, the council won't get back to you.

"At the same time, I count myself lucky that I have this place."

Scott also volunteers at a nearby shelter run by Homeless Project Scotland, which is itself under threat of closure due to a rise in crime near its premises.

Four homeless deaths in Scotland a week, data suggests

Record high number of homeless people in temporary housing

Three years ago, Glasgow City Council declared a housing emergency .

It followed the example set by Edinburgh, where a housing shortage saw even worse pressure on homelessness services and temporary accommodation.

Since 2023, the strain on housing services in Scotland's biggest city has steadily grown.

According to the latest data, last September saw Glasgow record its highest ever total of households in temporary homeless accommodation, at 4,332.

That included a record number of children - 3,225.

While the number of new applications to be made homeless fell between March and September last year, the number of open cases - people stuck in the system waiting to be housed - also hit a record high at 6,734.

The figures covering the period until March 2026, which will be published today, are not expected to show much improvement.

Samantha Lyle has been employed by the city's health and social care partnership as a social care worker for five years.

She works within its enhanced outreach support team, and said they were "absolutely inundated" with demand.

We met her at the Simon Community Hub in Argyle Street, a one-stop-shop for homelessness and addiction support run by the charity and partly funded by the local authorities.

There was a small queue of homeless applicants, some of whom were from overseas.

"I think with leave to remain and the refugees, the hub is a focal point so we could have hundreds through the doors," said Lyle.

"But I think in general terms the homelessness services are extremely busy, a lot busier... Case loads are extremely high and there are a lot more complexities with those presenting as homeless."

Her job is also about problem-solving. In one of the hub's booths, a woman discussed her situation with Lyle.

The woman, who has mental health problems and was living in Edinburgh, was given a tenancy in Glasgow in January - but something has gone wrong.

"She's come in, basically saying that men are coming in and threatening her," Lyle said.

"They are banging on her door, assaulting her, entering her flat without her permission.

"This is what we could call 'cuckooing' - the tenancy or the flat has been overrun by unknown individuals for many reasons.

Lyle said that a lot of people the service worked with could not maintain a tenancy or independent living.

"For us, a lot of it is down to a lack of services that mean we'd be able to house people with complex needs," she said.

Ricky Bell, the new leader of Glasgow City Council, said they needed to "start acting as though this is an emergency - and that means doing things slightly differently".

During his campaign to run the council, Bell said he believed Glasgow was "carrying the burden" of the UK's policy on housing refugees .

In 2023, council officers told the BBC that Glasgow's housing emergency had been exacerbated by attempts by the Home Office to clear the backlog of people awaiting asylum decisions.

Some applications were streamlined, meaning a higher number of claimants were given leave to remain.

They were asked to leave their Home Office-provided accommodation and presented to local homelessness services.

Between April and September 2025, almost half of Glasgow's homeless applications came from those with refugee or leave to remain status .

"That's causing a real problem for us in terms of how we cope with that significant increase in the volume of people that are coming," said Bell.

"We don't have the infrastructure. We don't have enough ability to put these people in temporary accommodation.

"We don't have enough houses to give them all permanent houses."

He wants the UK government to pause its asylum dispersal scheme to allow the city "to be able to refocus itself".

"I think we were coping relatively well with the homeless people, the volumes of homeless people that were coming through before the UK government changed that there," he added.

In 2022, the Scottish parliament voted to abandon the local connection rule for homelessness applicants.

While it didn't apply to refugees, it meant that if someone with no links to Glasgow applied for homelessness support in the city, the council could refer them back to some other part of Scotland where they did have connections - like work or family history.

But Bell said the policy needed a rethink.

"We are now seeing people coming from the rest of the UK and Northern Ireland to Glasgow because the legislation is more sympathetic to people here and it treats them better," he said.

"I've always been one of these people who said that governments, whether it's local government or national government or the UK government, should stick to their lane.

"What I'm going to say to them is if you want to have that policy you have to fund it and at the moment they're not doing that properly. That's just unsustainable."

He said Glasgow could not be responsible for the vast majority of the homeless problem in Scotland without being funded to do that.

The Scottish government said the "acute pressures" facing Glasgow City Council had been "significantly exacerbated" by the UK government's handling of the situation.

A spokesperson said: "We have repeatedly called on the UK government to properly fund local authorities facing these additional pressures and to address the impact Home Office policies are having on local housing and homelessness systems."

They added Glasgow City Council was being provided with more than £123m through the Affordable Housing Supply Programme, alongside additional support for the resettlement of refugees.

The Scottish government said it had committed to investing up to £4.9bn over the next four years to support the delivery of around 36,000 affordable homes across the country.

The UK government said it was closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

A spokesperson said: "This is helping to ease the burden on local communities and taxpayers, with asylum costs down by £1bn since the general election.

"As we progress with this work, we will fairly house asylum seekers across the country.

"That means engaging with local authorities to reduce the impact on communities including around the transition from asylum accommodation."

articles.title: CIA director meets with Zelensky at airport in Ireland
articles.summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at an airport in Ireland on Monday as the two waited for their planes to be refueled en route to the U.S., a person familiar with the meeting told The Hill. Ratcliffe and Zelensky briefly met at Shannon Airport, said the source, who declined to…
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at an airport in Ireland on Monday as the two waited for their planes to be refueled en route to the U.S., a person familiar with the meeting told The Hill.

Ratcliffe and Zelensky briefly met at Shannon Airport, said the source, who declined to elaborate on what the two officials discussed.

Ratcliffe was on his way back to the U.S. after meeting with Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi on Sunday, where the two discussed a variety of topics , including the Iran war, intelligence cooperation, the Gaza ceasefire, the Sudanese civil war, Somalia and more.

Zelensky was flying to New York City, where he is set to partake in meetings with world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly .

The Ratcliffe-Zelensky meeting, which was reported earlier by Reuters, comes after the CIA director flew to Russia last month for an unannounced meeting with the Kremlin’s intelligence officials.

While President Trump described the Aug. 25 huddle with Russian officials as “semi-routine,” Ratcliffe reportedly warned Russia against potentially attacking NATO countries.

One European official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive meetings, previously told The Hill that the U.S. briefed allies regarding the meeting in Moscow and was focused, in part, on Ukraine.

articles.title: Mexico responded to a Spanish woman’s murder with urgency. Some say it’s not doing enough for female victims at home
articles.summary: The recent murder of a female foreign exchange student in central Mexico has cast international attention on the country’s high levels of violence against women.
articles.body: The recent murder of a female foreign exchange student in central Mexico has cast international attention on the country’s high levels of violence against women, prompting the Mexican government to act with an urgency that some say it often lacks in cases involving its own nationals. Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a 21-year-old student from Spain, was killed by a man during an armed robbery near a cultural center on September 12, just a month after she arrived in Mexico for her exchange program at the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos (UAEM), according to state prosecutor Fernando Blumenkron. His office said authorities on Thursday arrested a suspect, charging him with feminicide, a crime in which a woman is intentionally killed for reasons related to her gender. CNN is seeking to determine whether the suspect has legal representation and how he intends to plead. Tacoronte’s murder sparked outcry across Mexico, with hundreds of people protesting last week to demand justice for the Spaniard as well as thousands of Mexican women killed over the years – including other female students from UAEM in recent months. “Feminicide is definitely one of the biggest problems in Mexico,” said Paulina Garcia-Del Moral, an associate professor at Canada’s University of Guelph, whose research specializes in examining the intersection of law, gender and power in many countries, including Mexico. “It is a really large problem precisely because … impunity is rampant in Mexico for all kinds of crimes.” Mexico’s government, which CNN has contacted for comment, has insisted publicly that there will be “zero impunity” for feminicide. But many women say they feel vulnerable and are demanding more action from officials, particularly in states like Morelos, where Tacoronte was killed. Here’s how the crisis is affecting the country, how officials have responded to it, and what experts say still needs to be addressed. ‘We are very unprotected’ Mexico is considered one of the worst countries in the world for women’s security, ranking 147th out of 181 in the 2025/26 global Women, Peace and Security Index. Officials have reported more than 9,100 feminicide cases nationwide since 2016, including 382 between January to July of this year. In that six-month span, the state of Morelos had the second-highest rate of cases (1.97 per 100,000 women), according to official figures. “We are very unprotected in the state of Morelos, given the prevailing insecurity and the failure of the authorities to act,” rights activist Zayra Hernandez told CNN. Hernandez is a member of Young Women Against Institutional Violence (Morras contra la Violencia Institucional), a group that was formed by victims primarily of sexual violence within UAEM, where Tacoronte was a foreign exchange student. Hernandez said she had been sexually assaulted by a fellow student when she attended the university and was physically attacked by another schoolmate. “Of course, we walk around with great fear, knowing that at any moment we could be effectively assaulted,” she said. Garcia-Del Moral notes that feminicides can happen both in public and private settings – including as a result of domestic or intimate partner violence. There are many factors that contribute to violence against women in Mexico, experts say, including gender inequality, pervasive sexist tropes and a high rate of impunity for killing women. “The vast majority of femicide or homicide cases don’t result in the identification of a suspect and often don’t result in those suspects being brought to justice,” said David Shirk, a professor at the University of San Diego’s Department of Political Science and International Relations. If crimes go unpunished, Garcia-Del Moral argued, it sends a message that people can continue to kill women without consequences. How have officials responded? In Spain, high-level government officials condemned Tacoronte’s murder and demanded a thorough investigation. The Mexican government responded with a multi-agency operation involving the defense ministry, the navy, the national guard, the ministry of public security, as well as state and federal prosecutors. Many welcomed the response but some accused the government of being slower to act when its own citizens are killed. “That doesn’t happen on a day-to-day basis in Mexico, and certainly not for our female colleagues from Morelos,” said Hernandez. While it’s a commonly held view, data isn’t collected on the topic. Even so, experts say the heavy attention this case received likely pressured Mexico to act. “Are authorities more likely to be responsive to cases that receive a high degree of publicity? I think the answer is yes,” said Shirk. “And then the question is: Do cases involving foreign nationals generally get a higher level of publicity? I would say yes.” CNN has reached out to the Mexican secretariats of women and security for comment. On Friday, authorities in Jalisco state announced the arrest of a suspect in a different high-profile feminicide case involving a Mexican medical student, Karla Perez. Mexico’s Secretary of Security and Citizen Protection Omar Garcia Harfuch insisted Thursday that preventing feminicides is one of the government’s priorities. “When we have not succeeded in preventing a woman from becoming a victim of this violence, our obligation is to clarify the facts, apprehend those responsible, and combat impunity with all the force of the state,” he said on X when he announced the arrest of Tacoronte’s suspected killer. Investigators have charged the suspect with feminicide and will seek a maximum prison sentence of 70 years, the state prosecutor said. While “feminicide” and “femicide” are often used interchangeably in English to define the gender-based killing of women, Garcia-Del Moral said there were subtle differences between the two terms in the Mexican context, with “feminicide” focusing more on the broader, structural conditions that led to the crime. A feminicide case activates protocols that outline how prosecutors, police and forensic experts should carry out their investigations, emphasizing the use of a gender perspective, Garcia-Del Moral explained. Though Tacoronte’s killing is being treated as a feminicide in the early stages of the investigation, Shirk points out that in previous cases the criminal charge has sometimes been later changed to a homicide, which carries a shorter sentence. This can happen if prosecutors determine that they won’t be able to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that a suspect killed the victim because of her gender. In those instances, homicide may be a more viable alternative for prosecutors because “it’s much easier to prove that you killed someone than the fact that your motivation was gender-based or gender bias,” Shirk said. How have universities responded? UAEM, the Mexican university where Tacoronte was an exchange student, had demanded that prosecutors conduct “an immediate, thorough investigation with a strict gender perspective to guarantee justice and prevent impunity.” But activists also urged the school itself to take more action, with some criticizing it for what they say is a lack of protection for women. At least three female UAEM students were killed earlier this year before Tacoronte’s murder, according to the National Citizen Observatory on Feminicide, a renowned organization representing 40 organizations from 22 Mexican states that specializes in the issue. The school has protocols in place to try to prevent violence and discrimination against women on campus, but critics say it’s clearly not enough given the recent killings. CNN has contacted the university to see if it will take additional steps to protect students. Spain’s University of Granada (UGR), where Tacoronte was studying early childhood education, said it will not send students to the state of Morelos in the coming semester. “Three students who were scheduled to go there for the second semester will no longer be doing so because we have suspended those placements,” said Inmaculada Marrero Rocha, vice-rector for internationalization. Other UGR exchange students in different parts of Mexico have been offered a chance to return to Spain, but Marrero Rocha said they have chosen to stay. She said students who study abroad are briefed about security conditions in different countries and are advised to take precautions. Other international schools have previously suspended or limited study abroad programs in parts of Mexico due to security concerns. What more can be done? Garcia-Del Moral said the country must strengthen institutions to reduce impunity. She also advised the government to better train public servants to recognize how gender inequality shapes violence and “focus on transforming ways of viewing women.” Similarly, Hernandez said officials should view the crisis through a gender perspective rather than treating it as solely a security problem. For students and foreigners visiting Mexico, Shirk advised exercising caution and being informed about the risks there but noted that the country still has a lot to offer. “Every day, hundreds of thousands of people (are) going into Mexico and having a wonderful time, enjoying the culture, the food,” he said. Hernandez added that while Morelos’ security problems need to be addressed, its dignity should be recognized, as well. “Our community – the general population – is a very beautiful and dignified place,” she said. “Yet, in the face of this wave of insecurity … we are standing firm and resisting.”

articles.title: Traffic chaos in Perthshire villages after Google Maps glitch
articles.summary: The issue saw vehicles leave the A9 and travel through the Perthshire villages of Ballinluig, Tulliemet and Guay.
articles.body:
A Google Maps glitch has caused chaos after traffic was mistakenly diverted from the A9 to a single-track road between Dunkeld and Pitlochry.

The issue - which was first noticed on Friday - saw vehicles, including campervans, leave the trunk road and travel through the Perthshire villages of Ballinluig, Tulliemet and Guay.

On Saturday Transport Scotland posted on X on that Google Maps was falsely reporting the A9 as closed and was recommending an "inconvenient alternate route" when it remained open.

The problem now appears to be resolved but local residents said the inaccurate information left them worried and, in some cases, unable to leave their homes.

"People were just doing as Google said but the excessive speed was unbelievable," Joanne Boyne, who lives in Guay, told BBC Scotland News.

"Traffic was going in both directions so when cars came to a section where nobody could pass, everyone had to reverse."

She said the U163 road is a single-track road with no designated passing places.

The winding and narrow nature of the road and the overgrown trees and bushes make it unsafe to drive fast.

But over the weekend, she saw campervans, a large coach and cars with trailers - one towing a boat - all drive down it, some at speeds as fast as 40mph.

"We were really worried about trying to get to potential appointments or if there was an emergency," Boyle said.

The bumper-to-bumper traffic meant there would have been no space for an ambulance or fire engine to get past if something was to happen, which was a serious concern in the community.

Boyle's parents live about three miles away from her Tulliemet.

"My parents live on the road and they have not been able to leave their house since Friday - even to go for a walk - because it has been too dangerous," she said.

The drive from her house to her parents' house would normally take her about 10 minutes but, when she went to check on them at the weekend, it took her almost 45 minutes to get there.

Joanne added that she struggled to get to work at about 07:50 on Monday as there were three cars waiting to turn onto the road from the A9, which is unusual.

Laura Hansler, from the A9 Dual Action campaign group, said the bug was fixed after a member of the group contacted the Google Maps team in London.

But she said problems appear on Google Maps now and again but she did not know what causes them.

Laura added that Google Maps had previously shown incorrect speed limits on sections of the trunk road.

"It is not an old diversion that was never cancelled, it is one of these daft diversions that make no sense," she said.

"Sometimes it will tell you the road is closed because there has been a collision but sometimes Google Maps acts up for no reason."

Laura said people who drive on the A9 tend to use a satnav as a safety feature to avoid collisions and roadworks.

She added many of the diversion routes are unsuitable for large vehicles and volumes of traffic.

"People are using them proactively and on the A9 when someone sees a diversion, they automatically presume it is because something has happened," she said.

"If these maps are not updated, it will cause an accident, which was my biggest fear at the weekend.

Laura said she had been in touch with Transport Scotland and the Scottish government on several occasions about the issue.

But Transport Scotland told her it did not have a direct relationship or feed to satellite navigation providers, such as Google.

The campaign group is now seeking further response from the government on the problem and calling for action to be taken to prevent future incidents.

articles.title: Vet prescription fees to be capped under rule changes
articles.summary: Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online as part of the rule updates which surgeries have the coming months to bring in.
articles.body:
Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at £21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the coming months.

Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online, write price estimates ahead of treatment, and publish price lists for services as part of the rule updates.

The official competition watchdog has brought the measures into force after its investigation into the sector found prices had been rising at nearly twice the rate of inflation.

However, critics say the measures will hit independent vets hardest and will benefit the six firms that own more than two-thirds of practices.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) made its remedies for the sector legally binding as of Tuesday and vets have up to 12 months to bring all the changes in.

As well as capping prescription fees, other changes include:

Vet practices must publish a "comprehensive" price list for standard services – including consultations, common procedures, and cremation options

A written estimate must be provided in advance for any treatment expected to cost £500 or more, including aftercare costs, plus an itemised bill. Emergencies are the only exception to this

Vet businesses must make clear whether they are part of a group or an independent business

To help pet owners compare local practices, price and ownership information will be made available through the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons' "Find a Vet" service, which will share the data with third-party comparison sites.

The timelines for when vets need to bring in the fixes depends on the exact regulation and the group's size. The CMA sets it out here.

"The changes that are being required are changes that will help inform pet owners about prices," said CMA panel chair Martin Coleman.

However, Cate Titterton, the owner of an independent vet service in Saltburn, told BBC Your Voice the changes will make trips to the vets more expensive for customers.

"Veterinary practices still have to have a pharmacy that is fully stocked, so if we're not making that tiny profit on the drugs, we're going to have to make some profit elsewhere.

"So, things like services, consultations, surgeries – unfortunately, those prices are very, very likely to have to go up."

She believes there is "one clear winner" from this - larger vet groups and the corporates.

British Veterinary Association President Dr Rob Williams said veterinary practices were already largely working to the CMA's remedies, including the orders relating to complaints handling, price estimates for routine procedures and prescription costs.

"We've been clear with the CMA throughout its investigation that it must ensure its remedies do not disproportionately impact smaller, independent practices and we've pushed back where we've had concerns," Williams said.

Vet surgeries 'not interested in the animal'

One person hoping to see a cheaper more transparent market for vet services is Clive Di Giorgio, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice.

He says he was quoted thousands of pounds for treatment after a vet told him that a rash on his dog Louis' back was "definitely" a sign of cancer.

However, after going to a different vet surgery, he says he was told Louis' rash was not cancerous.

A treatment of steroids, antibiotics, and a spray cleared up the rash in two weeks, Clive says.

"You just don't feel as if when you go to the vets now they're interested in the animal," he says.

"You feel as if all the interest is how much money they can basically squeeze from you."

articles.title: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance
articles.summary: The phenomenon sees retirees spend all their money on enjoying life to the full.
articles.body:
Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".

While other retirees with a decent monthly pension income may choose to build up an inheritance for their children, Sarah, 64, and her husband Geoff are opting to spend their money on living life to the max.

"We like going to Scotland," says Sarah, a retired school administrator. "We've been down to Cambridgeshire, which was lovely. We go up to the Lake District quite regularly to a holiday cottage, and we're planning to go to Norfolk."

The couple, who live in the Yorkshire Dales, go on holiday four or five times a year, spending hundreds of pounds each time because, in Sarah's view, "you only have one opportunity at life".

They did recently sell their vintage Sunbeam Alpine sports car. But only so they could replace it with a more modern, sporty two-seater convertible, a Mazda MX-5.

"I'm of an age where I'm going to friends' and acquaintances' funerals, and I think you just need to live life and enjoy it while you can, because it's a very precious commodity," says Sarah.

Sarah and Geoff are part of a global personal finance phenomenon that has been dubbed "skiing", which stands for spending the kids' inheritance. It is challenging the notion that assets will get handed down to the next generation.

One in seven UK parents of children of all ages (15%) now plan to prioritise enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance, according to a March report by pension provider Standard Life.

And in the US, the number of people expecting to get an inheritance from their parents dropped to 20% last year, from 25% in 2024, according to a study by financial services firm Northwestern Mutual.

Sarah and Geoff have two adult daughters. One of them, Poppy, tells the BBC that she couldn't be happier that her parents are out and about having fun.

She firmly rejects the notion that she and her sister should expect an inheritance. "To me that's wild. It never even crossed my mind that I'll get money when my mum and dad die. I'd so much rather them do what they want to do."

Mike Ambery, retirement and savings director at Standard Life, believes that the move towards skiing in the UK has been driven by the disappearance of final-salary pensions, which provide guaranteed monthly pension payments that last for as long as the retiree lives.

Instead, more people in the UK now have what are called defined contribution pension pots, which can run out. Ambery argues that it's easier to be generous with a legacy if you know your retirement income will last as long as you need it.

He also points to pensioners wanting to simply enjoy themselves after a life of working.

"It's just having a little bit of indulgence to enjoy life. Let's face it, working life can be very hard for some people."

Not all retirees are well off, of course. In the UK, 16% of pensioners live in poverty, according to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation charity.

The figure for the US is 15.4%, newly released data shows.

But at the same time, UK pensioners have seen their disposable income, excluding housing costs, increase by more than that of non-pensioners over the last three decades, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank .

Some 69% of retirees in the UK have a private pension in addition to their state one, official figures show. In the US 56% of pensioners have a private pension.

Karen Green, 60, says she has been very upfront with her children. "I have been quite explicit to say there is unlikely to be a legacy because I'm anticipating spending it all."

Originally from Berkshire, Karen has lived in Provence in the south of France for the past 11 years, and spends more than £10,000 a year on holidays.

"This year, I'm going to a yoga retreat. I did one in March in Morocco," she says. "Then in October into November I'm going to Vietnam and Laos to do a little bit of a tour."

She describes herself as semi-retired, as she tops up her private pension by still doing some business consultancy work, the job she used to do full-time.

When it comes to how much money she has per month, she says that her income is the same as when she was working full-time. In addition to her pension and income from her part-time work, she gains 40% of her funds from renting out a property.

But Karen insists she's not "crazy with money" and likes "to get a deal".

Like Sarah Moorhouse she won't get her UK state pension until she is 67. That's currently a standard £12,547.60 a year for people who reached the state pension age after April 2016, but it is due to go up next year.

As a comparison, retirees in the US get state payments known as social security retirement benefits.

The maximum annual amount starting from the "full retirement age" of 67 is $49,824 (£36,993). However, people can choose to take a lower payment from the age of 62.

Matthew Loveless, a vice president at Northwestern Mutual, based in Ohio, says retirees need to be upfront with their adult children, some of whom might be expecting an inheritance that they intend to rely on.

Back in Yorkshire, Sarah is planning her next holiday. "I've worked hard all my life and I think I deserve to have a bit of free time and to be able to do nice things."
